title: They Stared Right at a Gorilla for 9 Seconds, Yet Half Saw Nothing
description:
In 1999 at Harvard University, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked viewers to count basketball passes by white-shirted players while a student in a full gorilla suit walked into the center of the game, thumped her chest, and stayed on screen for 9 seconds—and half of observers missed her completely (Perception, 1999). Follow-up eye-tracking proved non-noticers stared straight at the gorilla for a full second (Memmert 2006), and in 2013, 83% of expert radiologists missed a gorilla 48 times larger than a lung nodule embedded in chest scans (Drew, Võ & Wolfe 2013).

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Simons DJ, Chabris CF (1999) Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events. Perception 28(9): 1059-1074. https://doi.org/10.1068/p281059
- Memmert D (2006) The effects of eye movements, age, and expertise on inattentional blindness. Consciousness and Cognition 15(3): 620-627. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.concog.2006.01.001
- Drew T, Võ MLH, Wolfe JM (2013) The Invisible Gorilla strikes again: Sustained inattentional blindness in expert observers. Psychological Science 24(9): 1848-1853. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797613479386
